PrimeXBT assigns your company by where you live, and the Saint Lucia company has no regulator at all, so no legal leverage cap or close-out rule protects its clients. PrimeXBT does not serve US residents.

3. IUX

IUX is a CFD broker founded in 2016, and its website names one licensed company, IUX Markets (MU) Ltd, which the Financial Services Commission of Mauritius authorizes. Its place on the list comes from 1:3000 leverage on the Standard and Raw accounts, although it is the one broker that misses our license test.

Pros and Cons of IUX

The pros and cons of IUX come down to very high leverage at a low entry cost on one side, and a single offshore license on the other.

  • Very high leverage: IUX ranks second on this list for forex leverage.
  • Small deposit: The Standard account starts at $30.
  • Stated protection: IUX says you can never lose more than your balance.
  • Offshore license only: The IUX website shows no Tier-1 or Tier-2 license.
  • Jurisdiction limits: IUX says actual leverage depends on where you live.
  • Restricted markets: IUX does not target the EU, UK, Australia, or US.

IUX Leverage by Entity and Account Protections

IUX gives its 1:3000 leverage through IUX Markets (MU) Ltd under a Tier-3 regulator in Mauritius, and its protections come from IUX’s own policy rather than from a strict regulator.

EntityRegulatorTierMax FX leverageNBPMargin callStop-out
IUX Markets (MU) LtdFSC Mauritius (GB22200605)Tier-31:3000Yes40%20%

An IUX client gets no legal leverage cap or close-out rule. IUX does not target US residents.

4. IC Markets

IC Markets is a raw-pricing broker that now trades as IC, with an Australian company registered since 2007, IC Markets (EU) Ltd under CySEC, and Raw Trading Ltd in Seychelles. For the biggest ratio on the list, IC Markets stands alone at up to 1:5000 on major and minor currency pairs.

Pros and Cons of IC Markets

The pros and cons of IC Markets come down to the highest leverage here and low costs on one side, and offshore loss terms on the other.

  • Top leverage: IC offers 1:5000 on four of its five account types.
  • Low costs: The Raw Spread (MetaTrader) account charges $3.50 per lot per side.
  • No minimum deposit: Standard and Raw Spread accounts start from $0.
  • Offshore entity: The 1:5000 leverage comes from Raw Trading Ltd in Seychelles.
  • Lower leverage at size: Leverage falls in steps to 1:500 above 100 lots.
  • No margin call promise: IC’s terms say it has no duty to warn you before closing positions.

IC Markets Leverage by Entity and Account Protections

IC Markets gives 1:5000 only through Raw Trading Ltd under the Seychelles FSA, whose terms do not guarantee negative balance protection, while IC Markets (EU) Ltd caps retail clients at 1:30 with EU protections.

Clients outside the EU join Raw Trading Ltd, whose terms make a client pay any debit balance beyond the funds held unless the protection applies. IC does not serve US residents.

5. MultiBank

MultiBank is a broker group founded in 2005 that says more than 18 regulators supervise its companies, including ASIC, CySEC, BaFin, and the Monetary Authority of Singapore. Breadth of regulation is MultiBank’s case for a place here, and its Standard, Pro, and ECN accounts all list up to 1:1000.

Pros and Cons of MultiBank

The pros and cons of MultiBank come down to extra insurance and a low entry point on one side, and offshore loss terms on the other.

  • Excess insurance: A Lloyd’s of London policy covers MEX Atlantic clients up to $1,000,000 per account.
  • Low entry: The Standard account starts at $50.
  • One leverage level: All three accounts list 1:1000.
  • No loss cap: MEX Atlantic’s agreement warns that losses can exceed your initial investment.
  • No margin call promise: The agreement lets MultiBank close positions without a margin call.
  • Expensive ECN entry: The ECN account needs $10,000.

MultiBank Leverage by Entity and Account Protections

MultiBank’s international site lists 1:1000 under a client agreement issued by MEX Atlantic Corporation, licensed by CIMA in the Cayman Islands, and that agreement promises no negative balance protection.

International clients join MEX Atlantic, which has no legal 1:30 cap and requires clients to cover any margin shortfall.

6. BlackBull

BlackBull Markets is a broker headquartered in Auckland, whose New Zealand company holds an FMA derivatives issuer license, while BBG Limited serves international clients under the Seychelles FSA. Platform choice sets BlackBull apart, with TradingView, cTrader, both MetaTrader versions, and its own CopyTrader.

Pros and Cons of BlackBull

The pros and cons of BlackBull come down to wide platform choice and free account opening on one side, and no negative balance protection on the other.

  • Copy trading: BlackBull runs its own CopyTrader platform.
  • No minimum deposit: ECN Standard, Prime, and Prime+ all start at $0.
  • Equal leverage: Every account type allows up to 1:500.
  • No negative balance protection: BBG Limited makes the client liable for any deficit.
  • Same risk in New Zealand: Its New Zealand disclosure warns you may lose more than you deposit.
  • Early close-outs: BBG Limited may start closing positions below 100% margin.

BlackBull Leverage by Entity and Account Protections

BlackBull offers 1:500 through both its Seychelles and New Zealand companies, and neither one promises negative balance protection, the clearest protection gap on this list.

EntityRegulatorTierMax FX leverageNBPMargin callStop-out

International clients join BBG Limited, because the New Zealand company takes deposits only from New Zealand bank accounts. BlackBull does not accept US applications.

7. FP Markets

FP Markets is a multi-asset broker whose Australian company has been registered since 2005, with First Prudential Markets Pty Ltd under ASIC and First Prudential Markets Limited under the Seychelles FSA. Low-cost Raw pricing earns FP Markets a place here, with Raw spreads from 0.0 pips.

Pros and Cons of FP Markets

The pros and cons of FP Markets come down to low Raw costs and loss protection on one side, and offshore terms on the other.

  • Low Raw cost: The Raw account charges $3 per lot per side.
  • Negative balance protection: The Seychelles agreement protects clients against negative balances.
  • Tier-1 group license: First Prudential Markets Pty Ltd holds an ASIC license.
  • Offshore entity: The 1:500 leverage comes from the Seychelles company.
  • No margin call promise: The agreement says FP Markets has no duty to send margin calls.
  • Wider Standard spreads: The Standard account starts from 1.0 pips.

FP Markets Leverage by Entity and Account Protections

FP Markets gives 1:500 through First Prudential Markets Limited under the Seychelles FSA, whose agreement protects clients against negative balances, while its Australian company follows the 1:30 cap.

EntityRegulatorTierMax FX leverageNBPMargin callStop-out
First Prudential Markets LimitedFSA Seychelles (SD130)Tier-31:500YesNone promisedAt maintenance margin
First Prudential Markets Pty LtdASIC (AFSL 286354)Tier-11:30YesN/AStandard close-out

International clients sign the Seychelles agreement, which closes positions once equity falls to the maintenance margin. FP Markets does not serve US residents.

8. Eightcap

Eightcap is a forex and CFD broker whose Australian company has been registered since 2009, while Eightcap Global Limited serves international clients from the Bahamas. Chart-first traders are Eightcap’s audience, because you link your account through TradingView’s Trading Panel and place trades straight from the chart.

Pros and Cons of Eightcap

The pros and cons of Eightcap come down to clear margin rules and steady leverage on one side, and discretionary loss protection on the other.

  • Clear margin rules: Eightcap warns you at 80% and closes positions at 50%.
  • Steady leverage around news: Eightcap says it does not cut leverage during news events.
  • One-chart trading: You can draw, test, and trade on the same TradingView chart.
  • Discretionary protection: Eightcap Global may waive a negative balance, but it does not have to.
  • Higher entry: Accounts start at $100.
  • No guaranteed stops: Eightcap warns that stop-losses can slip in fast markets.

Eightcap Leverage by Entity and Account Protections

Eightcap gives 1:500 on forex through Eightcap Global Limited under the Securities Commission of The Bahamas, which covers negative balances only at its discretion, while Eightcap Pty Ltd under ASIC caps retail clients at 1:30.

EntityRegulatorTierMax FX leverageNBPMargin callStop-out
Eightcap Global LimitedSCB Bahamas (SIA-F220)Tier-21:500At Eightcap’s discretion80%50%
Eightcap Pty LtdASICTier-11:30YesN/AStandard close-out

Eightcap’s agreement lets it change leverage at its discretion. Eightcap does not offer CFDs to US residents.

Which Forex Broker Gives the Highest Leverage?

IC Markets gives the highest forex leverage on this list, up to 1:5000 on major and minor pairs through Raw Trading Ltd under the Seychelles FSA, followed by IUX at 1:3000. Here are the eight brokers ranked by top forex leverage:

RankBrokerMax FX leverage
1IC Markets1:5000
2IUX1:3000
3PrimeXBT1:1000 to 1:2000 (its pages differ)
4XM, MultiBank1:1000
6BlackBull, FP Markets, Eightcap1:500

The top number needs the right entity, account type, and position size. For traders asking which forex broker offers 1000 leverage, five brokers here qualify: IC Markets, IUX, PrimeXBT, XM, and MultiBank.

Is 1:5000 Leverage Possible?

Yes, 1:5000 forex leverage is possible at IC Markets on the Standard, Raw Spread (MetaTrader), Raw Pro, and Raw Pro+ accounts, but only through Raw Trading Ltd and only for the first 25 lots.

One standard lot of USD/JPY is $100,000, so at 1:5000 it needs just $20 of margin because the broker’s low margin requirements let a trader use very little capital to control a much bigger position, and a price move of 1 ÷ 5,000, or 0.02%, wipes that $20 out while leverage can magnify both profits and losses. Lower ratios are common too, so 1000x leverage is possible at the five brokers named above, with $100 of margin per lot.

The account closes even sooner, because IC’s 50% stop-out arrives after a 0.01% move against a fully used margin, and as exposure rises and trades become larger positions, the broker reduces maximum leverage to limit excessive risk.

Advertised vs Real Leverage: When Brokers Cut Your Leverage

The leverage on a broker’s homepage is only the advertised maximum, and the leverage on your trade can be much lower because the real ratio changes with position size, total exposure, and jurisdiction.

Position size: Some brokers cut leverage as the position grows, and IC applies 1:5000 to the first 25 lots, 1:3000 up to 50 lots, 1:1000 up to 100 lots, and 1:500 above that. This tiered approach can give experienced traders more control over margin use, but it also reduces leverage on larger positions as exposure grows.

News and weekends: IC drops leverage on forex and metals to about 1:200 for new positions from 15 minutes before to 1 minute after high-impact news. The same cut runs from 1 hour before Friday’s close to 30 minutes after Monday’s open. XM says its margin stays the same overnight and at weekends, and Eightcap says it does not cut leverage for news.

Entity and residence: The company that opens your account sets your cap, so IC’s EU clients get 1:30 while its Seychelles clients can get 1:5000.

Before you trade, check three things on the broker’s leverage page:

  1. Tiers: Check how leverage impacts margin and overall exposure at each tier.
  2. Time windows: Note when news and weekend rules apply and the reduced ratio.
  3. Entity: Confirm which company and regulator will hold your account.

How We Chose These Brokers

We chose high leverage brokers in two steps, first with a gate that every broker should pass and then with a four-point rating.

The gate had three tests, and two brokers did not clear all of them:

  • Leverage: Every broker offers at least 1:500 on forex at one entity or more.
  • License: Seven brokers hold a Tier-1 or Tier-2 license at group level, but IUX shows only an FSC Mauritius license.
  • US residents: Seven brokers say they do not accept US residents, but MultiBank’s international terms do not mention US clients.

We then rated each broker on four points:

  • Entity transparency: We check how clearly leverage and protection are tied to a company.
  • Trading costs: We compare spreads, commissions, and minimum deposits.
  • Platforms and risk tools: We check platforms and stop-loss tools across each trading style, from beginners to active traders.
  • Account conditions: We compare margin rules and leverage policies.

Negative balance protection and stop-out levels are shown, not gated, because most high-leverage offers sit in offshore entities where these protections are thin.

We built the tables from broker websites, client agreements, and regulator pages, and this review covers broker terms and protections only because we did not open a live account or fund one.

Regulator Tiers We Used

Regulator tiers matter because the regulator, not the brand, decides your leverage cap, your close-out rule, and whether your losses can exceed your deposit.

In the United States, retail forex brokers must register with the CFTC and NFA to protect traders. U.S. retail forex firms must also maintain at least $20 million in regulatory capital, which supports transparent pricing and supervision.

We grouped regulators by the client protections that define each tier in this article:

TierExample regulatorsWhat it usually means for client protection
Tier-1FCA, ASIC, CySEC, BaFinRetail leverage cap, required negative balance protection, set close-out level
Tier-2FSCA, CIMA, FMA, SCBFull local license, but not the full Tier-1 set of retail rules
Tier-3FSA Seychelles, FSC Belize, FSC Mauritius, VFSCOffshore license, with protection set mostly by broker policy

The tier belongs to the entity, not the brand, so a group with a Tier-1 license can still open your account through its Tier-3 company.

What Is High Leverage in Forex?

High leverage in forex is a double edged sword, but it can be an advantage when used carefully because it lets you control a position many times larger than the margin deposit the broker holds for it.

The 1:30 benchmark comes from regulators in the UK, the EU, and Australia, where that cap applies to FX majors, while lower caps apply to FX minors. Ratios such as 1:500 or 1:1000 are available only from entities outside those rules.

How Leverage and Margin Work

Leverage and margin follow one formula, margin equals position size divided by leverage, so higher leverage lowers the cash you set aside for the same trade. For one standard lot of USD/JPY, which is $100,000 of currency, the margin at three leverage levels is:

LeverageMargin for 1 standard lot ($100,000)
1:100$1,000
1:500$200
1:1000$100

Higher leverage frees cash, but each price move still costs the same dollars.

Margin Call and Stop-Out Explained

Margin level is your equity divided by your used margin, and a broker sends a margin call at one level and closes positions with a stop-out at a lower one.

This table shows the price move that triggers stop-out on a fully used margin, using (1 − stop-out level) ÷ leverage:

Leverage0% stop-out20% stop-out50% stop-out
1:1001%0.8%0.5%
1:5000.2%0.16%0.1%
1:10000.1%0.08%0.05%
1:50000.02%0.016%0.01%

XM and IUX close at 20%, IC Markets, BlackBull, and Eightcap at 50%, and PrimeXBT’s MT5 accounts at 0%. A 0% stop-out keeps positions open until the margin is gone, so a sudden gap has no buffer left and can push the balance below zero.

Pros and Cons of High Leverage

High leverage helps a disciplined trader use less cash per trade, but it also makes every loss bigger compared with the account’s equity.

Pros of High Leverage Trading

The pros of high leverage trading come from tying up less margin per trade, which creates practical benefits in how far a small balance can go.

  • Lower margin: Each position ties up less of your balance.
  • Small starting deposit: A few hundred dollars can open a standard lot.
  • More open positions: Freed margin can support trades across more assets or different asset classes.
  • Short-term trading: This can appeal to some active traders using leveraged products carefully to trade small, fast moves.

Cons of High Leverage Trading

High leverage can create significant risk because it magnifies losses on leveraged products, even when you only post a small amount of margin.

  • Bigger losses: A small move takes a large share of your equity, so you should consider whether you can afford the loss if the market moves fast.
  • Faster stop-out: At 1:1000 and a 50% stop-out, a 0.05% move closes a fully used position.
  • Higher costs relative to equity: Spreads and swaps are charged on the full position.
  • Weaker protection: Many retail traders use offshore brokers to access higher leverage, but those firms may leave them exposed to significant risk if losses exceed the balance.

Is High Leverage Trading Safe?

No, high leverage trading is not safe by default, because a small price move causes a large loss, and your real risk depends on position size, your entity’s regulator, and its protections. Many brokers disclose that roughly 74% to 89% of retail accounts lose money when trading CFDs, while IC Markets (EU) Ltd reports 73.46% and IUX reports 76%.

The table compares what a Tier-1 entity must give you with what an offshore entity may give:

ProtectionTier-1 entity (FCA, ASIC, CySEC)Offshore entity
Leverage cap1:30 on major pairsUp to 1:5000
Negative balance protectionRequiredBroker policy, or none
Margin close-out50% in the EU and UKSet by the broker (0% to 50%)
Loss-rate risk warningRequiredOptional

Regulated forex brokers with high leverage are therefore groups, where a Tier-1 company serves local clients and an offshore one gives the leverage, which is why regulated groups separate tighter retail protections from offshore high-leverage entities for forex trading.

Can You Lose More Than Your Deposit?

Yes, you can lose more than your deposit unless negative balance protection covers your entity and account, because a fast market can close your position past the point where your balance hits zero.

Price gaps and slippage cause this. When the Swiss National Bank dropped its minimum euro rate for the franc in 2015, EUR/CHF jumped past many traders’ stop levels, so their orders filled at far worse prices.

On this list, XM, PrimeXBT, IUX, and FP Markets state negative balance protection for their high-leverage accounts, while Eightcap applies it at its discretion. IC Markets makes clients pay any debit balance unless the protection applies, and BlackBull and MEX Atlantic leave losses beyond the deposit with the client.

Is 1:1000 Leverage OK?

1:1000 leverage is OK only for positions that are very small compared with your equity, or for traders who accept that a tiny move can close the account.

At 1:1000, a 0.1% move against a fully used margin wipes out the whole margin, and a 50% stop-out closes the trade after just 0.05%.

The fix is to watch effective leverage, which is position size divided by equity, so a $10,000 position on a $2,000 balance runs at 5:1.

How to Manage Risk Management When Using High Leverage

The safest way to use high leverage is through risk management, with position sizing based on the loss you accept on each trade rather than the maximum the broker allows.

  1. Size by effective leverage: Choose your position size divided by equity before you trade.
  2. Set a stop-loss: A stop-out closes positions at a much larger loss.
  3. Avoid margin windows: Do not open trades just before high-impact news or the weekend close.
  4. Allow for slippage: Stops can fill at a worse price in fast markets. Traders should also check execution quality, because faster and cleaner fills can reduce slippage during volatility.
  5. Choose an entity with negative balance protection: It caps your worst case at your deposit. It is essential to match position size and stop placement to your risk tolerance.

A simple rule of thumb is to risk about 1% of equity per trade. With a stop 0.5% from your entry, that rule gives a position worth twice your equity, or 2:1 effective leverage, far below any broker’s cap.

How to Choose a High Leverage Forex Broker

The right regulated broker depends on your trading style, the available assets, and the protections tied to the entity that will hold your account, so check these seven criteria before you open an account:

  • Which entity will hold your account: The entity sets your leverage and your rights.
  • Regulator tier of that entity: A higher tier usually means stricter client rules.
  • Negative balance protection for that entity: It limits your loss to your deposit.
  • Margin call and stop-out levels: They decide when you get a warning and when positions close.
  • Leverage policy: Leverage can fall with equity, size, or news and weekend windows.
  • Trading costs: Spreads and commissions are charged on the full position, including when trading CFDs where relevant across the broker’s markets.
  • Platforms and risk tools: Stop-losses and clear margin displays help you control risk, and some brokers offer proprietary platforms while others focus on MetaTrader, cTrader, or TradingView integrations.

Trading Costs Under High Leverage

Trading costs grow with the leverage you use across a wide spectrum of markets, not just forex, because spreads, commissions, and swaps are charged on the full position size, not on the margin you put up.

Say you have $1,000 of equity and the spread costs $10 on every $100,000 traded. At 1:100, a full-margin trade opens $100,000, so the spread takes 1% of your equity. At 1:1000, a full-margin trade opens $1,000,000, so the spread takes $100, or 10% of your equity, before the price moves. When comparing brokers, check for an extensive range of account and market options only after confirming the pricing is competitive and clear.

Raw accounts show this cost as a fixed commission, such as $3.50 per lot per side at IC Markets, so you can work out the cost before each trade.

Leverage Limits by Country

Leverage limits around the world are designed to protect traders by capping retail exposure, and the four regulators below cap major forex pairs between 1:30 and 1:50:

JurisdictionRegulatorMax retail leverage on major FX pairsNotes
United StatesCFTC and NFA1:50 (2% deposit)1:20 on other pairs (5% deposit)
United KingdomFCA1:3050% close-out, negative balance protection
European UnionESMA1:3050% close-out, negative balance protection
AustraliaASIC1:301:20 on minor pairs, negative balance protection

Seven brokers in this list say they do not accept US residents, and US rules keep retail forex leverage at 1:50 on FX majors and 1:20 on FX minors. Many offshore brokers claim to take US clients without proper authorization. It is essential to verify any firm in the NFA BASIC database before sending money, because unauthorized offshore firms can create significant risk. The legal route for US traders is an NFA-member retail forex dealer or futures commission merchant, or exchange-traded currency futures.

Offshore entities exist because of these caps, and their higher leverage comes with weaker protection. Some US traders may already access other assets such as stocks or futures domestically, but offshore forex leverage comes with fewer protections.

title: Formula 1’s 830 Million Fans Draw Forex and CFD Brokers to Global Sponsorships
summary:
Formula 1 has transformed into one of the world's fastest-growing sports
properties, reaching a global fanbase of more than 830 million people, a 12%
year-on-year increase. For brokers, the opportunity goes beyond brand
visibility, with partnerships increasingly becoming platforms for fan
engagement...
content:
Formula 1 has transformed into one of the world's fastest-growing sports properties, reaching a global fanbase of more than 830 million people, a 12% year-on-year increase. For brokers, the opportunity goes beyond brand visibility, with partnerships increasingly becoming platforms for fan engagement and brand activation.

The trend is particularly evident within the Forex and CFD sector, where an increasing number of brokers are leveraging F1 as a global marketing and brand-building platform. XMTrading, IC Markets, Libertex, Pepperstone, AvaTrade, INFINOX and Vantage are among the brands that have entered the F1 sponsorship landscape.

London's trading industry is coming home!

Meanwhile, FxPro stands out for the longevity of its involvement in the sport, with its current partnership with McLaren dating back to 2018, following earlier F1 team sponsorships with BMW Sauber and Virgin Racing.

According to Ampere Analysis, total Formula 1 sponsorship investment exceeded US$3 billion, with teams generating more than US$2 billion and Formula 1's commercial rights holders contributing the remaining US$1 billion.

SponsorUnited's Formula 1 Sponsorship Intelligence Report 2025 also highlights technology as the largest sponsoring sector, investing US$543 million, while financial services ranks as the second-largest category.

Team partnerships can command US$5 million–US$20 million per season, with high-profile partnerships potentially requiring significantly greater investment, making activation critical to maximising the value of the partnership.

Why Are Forex and CFD Brands Investing?

The growing presence of Forex and CFD brands in Formula 1 is unlikely to be coincidental.

As competition intensifies across the industry, firms are increasingly looking beyond traditional digital advertising to build stronger brand equity and earn traders' trust. Formula 1 provides a unique platform to achieve this through its global reach, premium positioning and year-round content ecosystem.

Formula 1 also embodies many of the same attributes that trading platforms seek to communicate: speed, precision, technology, continuous innovation and high-performance decision-making. This natural alignment allows sponsorships to feel authentic, creating stronger brand associations than traditional advertising alone.

What Makes Formula 1 Different?

1. Every Grand Prix Is a Unique Destination

Unlike traditional league competitions, where each match follows a similar format, every Formula 1 Grand Prix has its own identity.

Historic circuit venues such as Silverstone and Monza showcase the sport's rich heritage, while destination races in Monaco, Singapore, Miami, Las Vegas and Abu Dhabi offer completely different atmospheres and experiences.

Rather than repeating the same event every week, Forex and CFD firms gain a portfolio of unique destinations that can be tailored to different markets, client segments and business objectives throughout the season.

2. Formula 1 Is More Than a Sporting Event

Formula 1 has evolved into a lifestyle and entertainment platform rather than just a racing series. Race weekends increasingly combine elite motorsport with fine dining, luxury hospitality, live concerts, fashion, celebrity appearances and premium networking opportunities.

This broader ecosystem allows sponsors to engage audiences beyond traditional motorsport fans while positioning their brands alongside innovation, luxury and world-class experiences.

3. World-Class Hospitality Creates Business Value

Hospitality remains one of Formula 1's most powerful commercial assets. Experiences such as Paddock Club access, garage tours, pit lane walks, driver appearances and behind-the-scenes team access create unforgettable moments that few sports can match.

For Forex and CFD firms, these experiences provide valuable opportunities to strengthen relationships with introducing brokers, affiliates, institutional partners, VIP clients and prospective customers in a premium business environment where conversations often extend beyond the race itself.

4. One Partnership, a Truly Global Platform

For Forex and CFD brokers, growth rarely comes from a single region or market. Formula 1's truly global calendar gives brokers the opportunity to engage clients and business partners across North America, the GCC, Europe and Asia-Pacific, while its diverse hospitality offering allows brands to tailor experiences to different audiences, even within the same Grand Prix.

This enables brokers to build a consistent global brand while supporting regional customer acquisition, partner engagement and business development.

5. F1 Offers More Than Race-Day Exposure

Rather than relying on one-off promotions, brokers can keep partnerships relevant throughout the customer journey, making Formula 1 an always-on platform for brand building and customer engagement.

For instance, FxPro has used its McLaren partnership to create content-led activations, including its Strategy Debrief series, which provides behind-the-scenes insight into McLaren's race strategy and key decisions.

By bringing the team's expertise and decision-making process to audiences, the activation creates a natural connection between the high-stakes tactical decisions of F1 and the principles of precision and risk management in financial markets.

Pepperstone has taken a more experiential approach through its Aston Martin Aramco partnership, creating a range of client and partner experiences, including pit-lane dinners, Monaco yacht hospitality, driver meet-and-greets, garage tours and Silverstone track days.

These experiences give the broker a platform to deepen relationships with existing clients, create memorable touchpoints for prospects and engage business partners in a more personal setting.

Together, these examples illustrate how brokers can use F1 partnerships for more than brand visibility, creating ongoing opportunities to engage clients, prospects and partners throughout the season.

6. The Challenge of F1 Partnerships and Making Them Work

For brokers considering an investment in Formula 1, the first step is recognising that F1 is a truly global property. Unlike other sports sponsorships centred around relatively fixed home venues and regular matchday routines, every Grand Prix is a different operating environment.

The circuit, organisers, hospitality infrastructure, transport, local culture and surrounding events can all vary significantly. Delivering a premium guest experience therefore starts long before guests arrive at the track, from the first invitation and travel arrangements through to the final moment of the race weekend. The details matter.

There is also far more happening around a Grand Prix than the race itself. Concerts, fireside conversations, fan activities, paddock experiences and other events can create additional touchpoints throughout the weekend. For brokers hosting clients, prospects or business partners, these can become valuable components of a wider experience rather than simply being treated as ancillary benefits of the partnership.

The opportunity extends beyond the race weekend, too. Team factories, technical facilities and off-track access can create highly exclusive, money-can't-buy experiences. Fireside conversations with team principals, discussions with technical representatives, driver appearances and factory tours can give clients a different perspective on the sport while creating more meaningful engagement with the brand.

Perhaps most importantly, brokers should consider how the partnership can create value for both sides. The strongest partnerships are no longer simply about paying for rights and access; they can also involve integrating a broker's products, technology or services into the wider F1 ecosystem.

This creates the potential for two-way business case studies that demonstrate how the partnership delivers tangible value to the rights holder while giving the broker an authentic story to take to clients, prospects and relevant industry stakeholders.

Ultimately, making an F1 partnership work requires more than securing the rights. It requires understanding the complexity of the calendar, curating the experience around each race and finding ways for the brand and rights holder to create value together.

Final Thoughts

For Forex and CFD brands, the opportunity in Formula 1 goes well beyond securing visibility on a car or access to a race weekend. The global calendar, diverse hospitality, content opportunities and access to teams and talent create a platform that can be activated differently across markets and throughout the season.

But that opportunity also comes with complexity. Every Grand Prix presents a different environment, audience and set of possibilities, meaning the value of the partnership ultimately depends on how well a broker understands the ecosystem and connects it to its own commercial objectives.

The most effective F1 partnerships are therefore not simply sponsorships. They are platforms for creating experiences, building relationships and developing stories that have value for both the broker and the rights holder.

Formula 1 has transformed into one of the world's fastest-growing sports properties, reaching a global fanbase of more than 830 million people, a 12% year-on-year increase. For brokers, the opportunity goes beyond brand visibility, with partnerships increasingly becoming platforms for fan engagement and brand activation.

The trend is particularly evident within the Forex and CFD sector, where an increasing number of brokers are leveraging F1 as a global marketing and brand-building platform. XMTrading, IC Markets, Libertex, Pepperstone, AvaTrade, INFINOX and Vantage are among the brands that have entered the F1 sponsorship landscape.

London's trading industry is coming home!

Meanwhile, FxPro stands out for the longevity of its involvement in the sport, with its current partnership with McLaren dating back to 2018, following earlier F1 team sponsorships with BMW Sauber and Virgin Racing.

According to Ampere Analysis, total Formula 1 sponsorship investment exceeded US$3 billion, with teams generating more than US$2 billion and Formula 1's commercial rights holders contributing the remaining US$1 billion.

SponsorUnited's Formula 1 Sponsorship Intelligence Report 2025 also highlights technology as the largest sponsoring sector, investing US$543 million, while financial services ranks as the second-largest category.

Team partnerships can command US$5 million–US$20 million per season, with high-profile partnerships potentially requiring significantly greater investment, making activation critical to maximising the value of the partnership.

Why Are Forex and CFD Brands Investing?

The growing presence of Forex and CFD brands in Formula 1 is unlikely to be coincidental.

As competition intensifies across the industry, firms are increasingly looking beyond traditional digital advertising to build stronger brand equity and earn traders' trust. Formula 1 provides a unique platform to achieve this through its global reach, premium positioning and year-round content ecosystem.

Formula 1 also embodies many of the same attributes that trading platforms seek to communicate: speed, precision, technology, continuous innovation and high-performance decision-making. This natural alignment allows sponsorships to feel authentic, creating stronger brand associations than traditional advertising alone.

What Makes Formula 1 Different?

1. Every Grand Prix Is a Unique Destination

Unlike traditional league competitions, where each match follows a similar format, every Formula 1 Grand Prix has its own identity.

Historic circuit venues such as Silverstone and Monza showcase the sport's rich heritage, while destination races in Monaco, Singapore, Miami, Las Vegas and Abu Dhabi offer completely different atmospheres and experiences.

Rather than repeating the same event every week, Forex and CFD firms gain a portfolio of unique destinations that can be tailored to different markets, client segments and business objectives throughout the season.

2. Formula 1 Is More Than a Sporting Event

Formula 1 has evolved into a lifestyle and entertainment platform rather than just a racing series. Race weekends increasingly combine elite motorsport with fine dining, luxury hospitality, live concerts, fashion, celebrity appearances and premium networking opportunities.

This broader ecosystem allows sponsors to engage audiences beyond traditional motorsport fans while positioning their brands alongside innovation, luxury and world-class experiences.

3. World-Class Hospitality Creates Business Value

Hospitality remains one of Formula 1's most powerful commercial assets. Experiences such as Paddock Club access, garage tours, pit lane walks, driver appearances and behind-the-scenes team access create unforgettable moments that few sports can match.

For Forex and CFD firms, these experiences provide valuable opportunities to strengthen relationships with introducing brokers, affiliates, institutional partners, VIP clients and prospective customers in a premium business environment where conversations often extend beyond the race itself.

4. One Partnership, a Truly Global Platform

For Forex and CFD brokers, growth rarely comes from a single region or market. Formula 1's truly global calendar gives brokers the opportunity to engage clients and business partners across North America, the GCC, Europe and Asia-Pacific, while its diverse hospitality offering allows brands to tailor experiences to different audiences, even within the same Grand Prix.

This enables brokers to build a consistent global brand while supporting regional customer acquisition, partner engagement and business development.

5. F1 Offers More Than Race-Day Exposure

Rather than relying on one-off promotions, brokers can keep partnerships relevant throughout the customer journey, making Formula 1 an always-on platform for brand building and customer engagement.

For instance, FxPro has used its McLaren partnership to create content-led activations, including its Strategy Debrief series, which provides behind-the-scenes insight into McLaren's race strategy and key decisions.

By bringing the team's expertise and decision-making process to audiences, the activation creates a natural connection between the high-stakes tactical decisions of F1 and the principles of precision and risk management in financial markets.

Pepperstone has taken a more experiential approach through its Aston Martin Aramco partnership, creating a range of client and partner experiences, including pit-lane dinners, Monaco yacht hospitality, driver meet-and-greets, garage tours and Silverstone track days.

These experiences give the broker a platform to deepen relationships with existing clients, create memorable touchpoints for prospects and engage business partners in a more personal setting.

Together, these examples illustrate how brokers can use F1 partnerships for more than brand visibility, creating ongoing opportunities to engage clients, prospects and partners throughout the season.

6. The Challenge of F1 Partnerships and Making Them Work

For brokers considering an investment in Formula 1, the first step is recognising that F1 is a truly global property. Unlike other sports sponsorships centred around relatively fixed home venues and regular matchday routines, every Grand Prix is a different operating environment.

The circuit, organisers, hospitality infrastructure, transport, local culture and surrounding events can all vary significantly. Delivering a premium guest experience therefore starts long before guests arrive at the track, from the first invitation and travel arrangements through to the final moment of the race weekend. The details matter.

There is also far more happening around a Grand Prix than the race itself. Concerts, fireside conversations, fan activities, paddock experiences and other events can create additional touchpoints throughout the weekend. For brokers hosting clients, prospects or business partners, these can become valuable components of a wider experience rather than simply being treated as ancillary benefits of the partnership.

The opportunity extends beyond the race weekend, too. Team factories, technical facilities and off-track access can create highly exclusive, money-can't-buy experiences. Fireside conversations with team principals, discussions with technical representatives, driver appearances and factory tours can give clients a different perspective on the sport while creating more meaningful engagement with the brand.

Perhaps most importantly, brokers should consider how the partnership can create value for both sides. The strongest partnerships are no longer simply about paying for rights and access; they can also involve integrating a broker's products, technology or services into the wider F1 ecosystem.

This creates the potential for two-way business case studies that demonstrate how the partnership delivers tangible value to the rights holder while giving the broker an authentic story to take to clients, prospects and relevant industry stakeholders.

Ultimately, making an F1 partnership work requires more than securing the rights. It requires understanding the complexity of the calendar, curating the experience around each race and finding ways for the brand and rights holder to create value together.

Final Thoughts

For Forex and CFD brands, the opportunity in Formula 1 goes well beyond securing visibility on a car or access to a race weekend. The global calendar, diverse hospitality, content opportunities and access to teams and talent create a platform that can be activated differently across markets and throughout the season.

But that opportunity also comes with complexity. Every Grand Prix presents a different environment, audience and set of possibilities, meaning the value of the partnership ultimately depends on how well a broker understands the ecosystem and connects it to its own commercial objectives.

The most effective F1 partnerships are therefore not simply sponsorships. They are platforms for creating experiences, building relationships and developing stories that have value for both the broker and the rights holder.

title: USDD Reports Strong Treasury Performance, Growth in Key Metrics, and Ecosystem Expansion
summary: 30 October 2026 — British Virgin Islands — USDD has reported strong treasury performance in Q3 2026, alongside continued growth in key metrics, including circulating supply and total value locked (TVL). These latest milestones reflect the protocol’s expanding ecosystem, with growing multichain adopt...
content:
30 October 2026 — British Virgin Islands — USDD has reported strong treasury performance in Q3 2026, alongside continued growth in key metrics, including circulating supply and total value locked (TVL). These latest milestones reflect the protocol’s expanding ecosystem, with growing multichain adoption, new DeFi integrations, and broader opportunities for users to earn, transfer, and deploy USDD.

As a decentralized, overcollateralized stablecoin, USDD is focused on combining stability with practical utility. Let’s take a closer look at the key developments behind USDD’s recent growth.

USDD’s Growing Market Presence: New Milestones

According to a recent report jointly published by RWA Foundation and Token Terminal, USDD recorded the largest market capitalization increase among the top 10 stablecoin issuers during October 12–19, 2026. USDD’s market capitalization grew by $180.3 million, accounting for approximately 40% of the combined $449.1 million increase recorded by the top 10 issuers.

For comparison, Sky ranked second with an increase of $86 million, while United Stables recorded growth of $22.8 million. This performance highlights USDD’s strong momentum relative to other major stablecoin projects.

As of October 29, 2026, USDD’s circulating supply has also surpassed $1.48 billion, reinforcing its position as the largest decentralized stablecoin on TRON. Meanwhile, protocol TVL has reached $2.18 billion, reflecting the substantial value of assets supporting the ecosystem.

Beyond these figures, USDD’s expanding DeFi integrations and transfer solutions are creating more opportunities for users to put their stablecoins to work. This growing utility provides an important foundation for broader adoption.

Expanding Utility: More Ways to Earn and Transfer USDD

Beyond financial performance, USDD continues to expand its practical applications through new DeFi partnerships and transfer integrations. These developments focus on two important user needs: earning competitive yields and moving stablecoins conveniently.

More Earning Opportunities Across DeFi

USDD Earn allows users to deposit USDD and receive sUSDD, currently offering a base APY of 4% with flexible withdrawals and no fixed lockup period. Users can also explore additional earning opportunities through partner platforms.

USDD has partnered with Binance Wallet and Gate DEX to expand earning opportunities, while campaigns such as TRON DeFi Summer provide additional incentives for users, allowing them to maximize their earning opportunities. For experienced users, there are also advanced lending and looping strategies on Pendle and Morpho to further increase earning potential.

Together, these integrations give users more flexibility to choose strategies based on their investment preferences and risk tolerance. Yields are subject to change, and advanced DeFi strategies involve additional risks.

Making Transfers Easier with GasFree and TokenPocket

USDD is also making transfers simpler and more affordable through integrations with GasFree and TokenPocket. Both solutions allow users to pay supported transaction fees directly in USDD on TRON without separately holding TRX.

On August 17, 2026, GasFree integrated USDD, marking a significant step toward making USDD transfers simpler, more efficient, and more cost-effective for everyday on-chain use. USDD currently supports GasFree transfers on TRON. The wallets currently supporting GasFree access are TronLink, Guarda, Klever Wallet, and eDir. Through GasFree, USDD transfers have cost approximately 0.5 USDD per transaction, compared with approximately 1.5 USDT for comparable USDT transfers. 

TokenPocket provides another way to make USDD transfers simpler. With USDD supported as a network fee payment option on TokenPocket, users can keep their transfer activity centered around USDD. TokenPocket’s Gas Boost Season campaign has also offered a 50% gas fee subsidy for users paying gas with USDD, further reducing costs for eligible users.

These integrations help reduce friction for wallet-to-wallet transfers, payments, and everyday on-chain activities. By combining earning opportunities with convenient transfers, USDD is becoming more practical for users beyond simply holding or trading stablecoins.

Multichain Expansion: Growing Across TRON, Ethereum, and BNB Chain

USDD’s growing presence across TRON, Ethereum, and BNB Chain is another important part of its ecosystem development, allowing it to reach more users and connect with a broader range of DeFi applications. Ethereum, in particular, accounts for a significant share of USDD’s multichain supply. As of October 29, 2026, $329.94 million of USDD’s $1.48 billion total circulating supply is on Ethereum, representing approximately 22.3%. Supporting multiple networks allows USDD to reach more users and connect with a wider range of DeFi applications.

TRON remains a core ecosystem, with integrations such as Binance Wallet, GasFree, and TokenPocket supporting both earning and transferring. These applications strengthen USDD’s utility within TRON’s established stablecoin infrastructure.

On Ethereum and BNB Chain, USDD and sUSDD provide access to additional DeFi opportunities. This broader network presence allows users to explore different earning products, lending markets, and liquidity opportunities across ecosystems.

For USDD, multichain expansion is not simply about being available on more blockchains. It is about giving users more ways to put their assets to work and expanding the stablecoin’s practical applications.

Record Treasury Performance in Q3

As USDD expands its earning opportunities, transfer utility, and multichain presence, its financial performance and key protocol metrics are also showing steady progress, reflecting growth across both its ecosystem and treasury.

USDD’s latest Treasury Report in Q3 2026 revealed another strong quarter, with revenue reaching $9.70 million, up 26.7% quarter over quarter. The treasury balance also surpassed $30 million for the first time, reaching $31.24 million.

A major contributor to this performance was Smart Allocator, USDD’s on-chain asset allocation system, which generated $9.11 million in Q3 income. By deploying funds from USDD’s protocol capital across selected DeFi strategies, Smart Allocator supports the protocol’s approach to generating sustainable yields over the long term.

Its investment activities and performance are also publicly visible on-chain, allowing users to monitor how assets are allocated. Together, these results demonstrate USDD’s growing income-generating capabilities and commitment to transparency.

Explore USDD’s treasury and Smart Allocator data:

https://usdd.io/treasury

https://usdd.io/smart-allocator

Beyond the Numbers: What’s Next for USDD?

USDD’s recent milestones reflect progress across three key areas: growing market presence, stronger treasury performance, and expanding ecosystem utility.

With circulating supply surpassing $1.48 billion, protocol TVL reaching $2.18 billion, and Q3 treasury revenue totaling $9.70 million, USDD has demonstrated significant momentum. At the same time, integrations with treasured ecosystem partners such as Binance Wallet, Gate DEX, GasFree, and TokenPocket are expanding the ways users can earn and transfer USDD.

Looking ahead, continued development across TRON, Ethereum, and BNB Chain will create further opportunities to connect USDD with new applications and users. While future growth depends on market conditions and adoption, the latest milestones highlight USDD’s progress toward building a more accessible and useful decentralized stablecoin ecosystem.

Explore USDD’s latest developments: https://usdd.io/

title: “An FTMO Ticker Sounds Really Cool”: FTMO’s Founders on Launching Futures and How the Prop Giant Made Bankers Like Them
summary: Fourteen years ago, in a trading club at the Prague University of Economics and Business, Otakar Šuffner and Marek Vašíček discovered a shared affinity for futures trading. When they founded FTMO in 2015, though, they had to be pragmatic. The retail prop trading industry was in its infancy, and the ...
content:
Fourteen years ago, in a trading club at the Prague University of Economics and Business, Otakar Šuffner and Marek Vašíček discovered a shared affinity for futures trading. When they founded FTMO in 2015, though, they had to be pragmatic. The retail prop trading industry was in its infancy, and the founders lacked both the capital and the business experience to navigate the complexities of futures. Instead, they built their business around CFDs, leveraging local industry connections, and became one of the better-known players in the industry. A month ago, they finally returned to their original passion. “So the time basically came this year. I like to say that Apple is also not releasing their products first. So it just took time,” Šuffner jokes.

London's trading industry is coming home!

Launching futures is merely the latest step in a wider campaign for the prop firm giant, which includes managing the operational realities behind the massive acquisition of legacy broker OANDA, navigating a fractured regulatory landscape and outmanoeuvring market volatility and predatory payout syndicates – all to build what they describe as a global “trading powerhouse.”

Futures Are Hot Now

Among the most intriguing shifts currently unfolding in the space is that futures-based prop offerings are becoming a new darling for funded traders. There’s good reason: industry pricing data indicate that a $100,000 futures evaluation costs roughly $190 on average, compared with about $420 for a $100,000 CFD/FX one.

Unsurprisingly, Šuffner notes that futures “were highly requested from our clients.”

Futures had typically achieved these lower entry costs through a single-phase, subscription-style model. FTMO is following the same traditional model for its futures prop offering. Šuffner doesn’t want to speak to why others have abandoned the subscription model, but says, “We are always focusing on ourselves; we asked our clients what product they want to trade and we ended up with our current offering.”

Read more: Tradeify Co-Founders: “Difficult to Enter” Futures Prop; Subscription Ditch “Barely Moved Revenue”

The firm is determined to treat futures as a core business rather than an offering on the side, which means confronting established US incumbents like Topstep. Launching the product required a dedicated team and significant capital investment, essentially creating a new business next to their CFDs. However, Vašíček subtly downplays the friction. “I don’t think that the entry barriers are that high as in the regulated business, right?” he observes.

Still, while the global hub for futures trading is the US, the founders have been surprised by the international demand. “I was expecting that it would be US-heavy, but we have pretty much global customers, so at least for me it was very interesting,” Vašíček notes.

“We Made Those Bankers Like FTMO”

Like many in both the prop and broker space, FTMO is attempting to build a throughline, where a user can progress seamlessly from funded evaluations to a retail brokerage account, and eventually to a professional one.

The founders reveal that they initially explored acquiring smaller, regionally regulated brokers in Europe and Australia, and then planned to build this brokerage arm organically, hiring industry veterans in late 2024, including ex-Skilling CEO Michael Kamerman.

When the opportunity to acquire OANDA, which was globally established with licenses across most major hubs, from private equity firm CVC emerged, Vašíček admits his first reaction was to ask his co-founder, “‘Are you crazy?’ Then we realised that if we are serious about what we are doing, this is the one and only opportunity to have a global approach,” he explains.

Negotiating with elite private-equity dealmakers was an intense education for the founders, testing their operational maturity. “It was kind of eye-opening,” Šuffner says. "We were scheduling the calls at 3:00 am.”

FTMO secured a massive US$250 million syndicated credit line led by UniCredit, a significant milestone for a firm whose only previous corporate debt was a minor loan for mobile phones. “We made those bankers like FTMO and received the financing in record time for the Czech Republic,” Šuffner says.

Convincing conservative Czech bankers to finance the buyout – together with cash reserves, OANDA was acquired for about US$422 million – was only half the battle. Securing global regulatory approval took nearly ten months. Financial watchdogs scrutinised the founders heavily.

“They were very thorough; they were asking about our eye colour, our weight,” Šuffner recalls.

Vašíček chimes in, “Our compliance team knows absolutely everything about the two of us.”

Ultimately, they consider the deal as proof that a modern prop firm could meet the exacting standards of traditional finance. Vašíček says, “This is a great message for the industry, that a modern prop trading firm was able to prove to all parties that something serious like this could happen.”

“Credibility Is Not Done in Two Days; It’s Something You Need to Live By”

The model of FTMO to become what it calls a “trading powerhouse” has seen varying degrees of success elsewhere.

For one, platform providers have made launching prop firms effortless, leading to a flood of copycat firms vying for the same pie. The model also faces a threat from organised hedging groups that game these evaluation systems.

Related: Inside the 800-Member Trading Cartel Bleeding Prop Firms Dry

Platform providers have even tweaked their backends to account for hedging. For example, FPFX Tech, which provides the infrastructure for over 150 prop firms, has added risk-monitoring tools designed to flag abusive trading behaviour, including hedging.

“It’s something we need to take care of, but we built a lot of human capital and know-how on how it needs to be handled,” Vašíček says.

He also sees these ‘payout syndicates’ as unfair to users who follow the rules. He notes that back in university, they failed to secure jobs at traditional proprietary firms because, in his view, their CVs didn't meet the Ivy League criteria. “Prop firms are an opportunity, pretty much a life-changing opportunity, because I can become a trader. Now nobody cares about the pedigree,” he notes.

The founders believe that integrating FTMO’s model with OANDA’s 30-year positioning and reputation gives them a unique structural advantage in succeeding where others are failing. “Credibility is not done in two days; it’s something you need to live by,” Vašíček observes.

Regulation? What About It?

In 2024, the industry experienced a supply-chain shock when MetaQuotes abruptly revoked platform licenses from firms sub-leasing its software to serve US prop clients. The disruption prompted several prop firms to acquire small regulated brokerages simply to secure direct software licenses. Šuffner, though, maintains that FTMO’s acquisition of OANDA was never about that. “It was really about making the group stronger and delivering broader services,” he explains.

While prop trading appears to have fallen from ESMA’s priority list – the Paris-based agency having begun preliminary reviews in 2024 – the Dutch financial regulator recently ruled in January that instant funding accounts offered by a firm named Unfunded constituted CFD trading. As such, the firm was operating without a proper MiFID II license. The decision was upheld in court; it marks the first instance a European regulator has equated prop trading with investment services.

Šuffner notes that they have been closely monitoring this case, remaining attentive to potential regulatory developments and their broader implications for the industry.

Still, neither appears particularly worried about regulation, an attitude that is seemingly informed by their many interactions with watchdogs. Aside from the OANDA dealings, Šuffner notes that they “received a letter from the Spanish regulator” to explain their offering. Other regulators also have made inquiries, including ASIC.

The firm also has a substantial financial buffer to navigate any cost increases inside an emerging regulatory environment. In 2025, it reported revenues of approximately $420 million, representing a 31% year-on-year growth. “A regulated environment is a higher barrier, right? That means that there will be no hundreds of prop firms, but maybe tens of prop firms will remain,” Vašíček says.

Nonetheless, Šuffner wonders about the need to regulate simulated trading. “Regulation is here to protect the client, for good reason,” he says. “With prop firm clients, they are buying a service for a much smaller amount that they basically deposit money with a brokerage firm. So, is there even something to regulate?”

Among the most intriguing shifts currently unfolding in the space is that futures-based prop offerings are becoming a new darling for funded traders. There’s good reason: industry pricing data indicate that a $100,000 futures evaluation costs roughly $190 on average, compared with about $420 for a $100,000 CFD/FX one.

Unsurprisingly, Šuffner notes that futures “were highly requested from our clients.”

An IPO in the Horizon?

Despite record top-line growth, 2025 tested the firm's profitability. FTMO’s net income fell by 59% to roughly $37.5 million, a drop attributed to extreme market volatility. What with President Trump's dizzying tariff announcements, tech-sector anxieties and general geopolitical friction, it made predicting where the chips would fall difficult. FTMO missed its projected trader payout targets by 82%.

Interestingly, Šuffner treats this primarily as an accounting variance. “I honestly didn’t know about it. I just saw it in the articles,” he says. “It’s an accounting number, but from a company point of view is not something that would harm us in any way.”

As they navigate these market conditions, the founders are determined to conduct business on their own terms. They want to distance FTMO from the aggressive, lifestyle-focused marketing that proliferates in the industry.

“We never had aggressive marketing, never promised cars, dreams and miracles that are done in four days,” Vašíček emphasises. “For us, it is important to still stay FTMO. We are here for the long term. So we feel this sense of accountability and we want to do serious business and provide great service for the customers.”

For now, OANDA and FTMO are kept as two businesses with distinct management teams, though both founders serve as co-CEOs overseeing the overarching structure, a role Vašíček admits is demanding, yet exciting. Vašíček notes that while they are keeping an eye on new developments like prediction markets, they remain focused on their own roadmap rather than moving at the pace dictated by others. “Like every other business, we need to look around and always think about what's the future so we don't end up being dinosaurs,” he says.

Without shareholders pressing them, they have the freedom to remain patient and move to the beat of their own drum. As Šuffner highlights, “We own 100% of FTMO and OANDA.”

While the founder mentioned in 2023, during an interview with Czech media outlet SZ, that going public did not make sense at the time, they remain open to the possibility, including any other forms of outside investment.

“An FTMO ticker sounds really cool,” Šuffner says, only half-joking.

The firm is determined to treat futures as a core business rather than an offering on the side, which means confronting established US incumbents like Topstep. Launching the product required a dedicated team and significant capital investment, essentially creating a new business next to their CFDs. However, Vašíček subtly downplays the friction. “I don’t think that the entry barriers are that high as in the regulated business, right?” he observes.

Still, while the global hub for futures trading is the US, the founders have been surprised by the international demand. “I was expecting that it would be US-heavy, but we have pretty much global customers, so at least for me it was very interesting,” Vašíček notes.

“We Made Those Bankers Like FTMO”

Like many in both the prop and broker space, FTMO is attempting to build a throughline, where a user can progress seamlessly from funded evaluations to a retail brokerage account, and eventually to a professional one.

The founders reveal that they initially explored acquiring smaller, regionally regulated brokers in Europe and Australia, and then planned to build this brokerage arm organically, hiring industry veterans in late 2024, including ex-Skilling CEO Michael Kamerman.

When the opportunity to acquire OANDA, which was globally established with licenses across most major hubs, from private equity firm CVC emerged, Vašíček admits his first reaction was to ask his co-founder, “‘Are you crazy?’ Then we realised that if we are serious about what we are doing, this is the one and only opportunity to have a global approach,” he explains.

Negotiating with elite private-equity dealmakers was an intense education for the founders, testing their operational maturity. “It was kind of eye-opening,” Šuffner says. "We were scheduling the calls at 3:00 am.”

FTMO secured a massive US$250 million syndicated credit line led by UniCredit, a significant milestone for a firm whose only previous corporate debt was a minor loan for mobile phones. “We made those bankers like FTMO and received the financing in record time for the Czech Republic,” Šuffner says.

Convincing conservative Czech bankers to finance the buyout – together with cash reserves, OANDA was acquired for about US$422 million – was only half the battle. Securing global regulatory approval took nearly ten months. Financial watchdogs scrutinised the founders heavily.

“They were very thorough; they were asking about our eye colour, our weight,” Šuffner recalls.

Vašíček chimes in, “Our compliance team knows absolutely everything about the two of us.”

Ultimately, they consider the deal as proof that a modern prop firm could meet the exacting standards of traditional finance. Vašíček says, “This is a great message for the industry, that a modern prop trading firm was able to prove to all parties that something serious like this could happen.”

“Credibility Is Not Done in Two Days; It’s Something You Need to Live By”

The model of FTMO to become what it calls a “trading powerhouse” has seen varying degrees of success elsewhere.

For one, platform providers have made launching prop firms effortless, leading to a flood of copycat firms vying for the same pie. The model also faces a threat from organised hedging groups that game these evaluation systems.

Related: Inside the 800-Member Trading Cartel Bleeding Prop Firms Dry

Platform providers have even tweaked their backends to account for hedging. For example, FPFX Tech, which provides the infrastructure for over 150 prop firms, has added risk-monitoring tools designed to flag abusive trading behaviour, including hedging.

“It’s something we need to take care of, but we built a lot of human capital and know-how on how it needs to be handled,” Vašíček says.

He also sees these ‘payout syndicates’ as unfair to users who follow the rules. He notes that back in university, they failed to secure jobs at traditional proprietary firms because, in his view, their CVs didn't meet the Ivy League criteria. “Prop firms are an opportunity, pretty much a life-changing opportunity, because I can become a trader. Now nobody cares about the pedigree,” he notes.

The founders believe that integrating FTMO’s model with OANDA’s 30-year positioning and reputation gives them a unique structural advantage in succeeding where others are failing. “Credibility is not done in two days; it’s something you need to live by,” Vašíček observes.

Regulation? What About It?

In 2024, the industry experienced a supply-chain shock when MetaQuotes abruptly revoked platform licenses from firms sub-leasing its software to serve US prop clients. The disruption prompted several prop firms to acquire small regulated brokerages simply to secure direct software licenses. Šuffner, though, maintains that FTMO’s acquisition of OANDA was never about that. “It was really about making the group stronger and delivering broader services,” he explains.

While prop trading appears to have fallen from ESMA’s priority list – the Paris-based agency having begun preliminary reviews in 2024 – the Dutch financial regulator recently ruled in January that instant funding accounts offered by a firm named Unfunded constituted CFD trading. As such, the firm was operating without a proper MiFID II license. The decision was upheld in court; it marks the first instance a European regulator has equated prop trading with investment services.

Šuffner notes that they have been closely monitoring this case, remaining attentive to potential regulatory developments and their broader implications for the industry.

Still, neither appears particularly worried about regulation, an attitude that is seemingly informed by their many interactions with watchdogs. Aside from the OANDA dealings, Šuffner notes that they “received a letter from the Spanish regulator” to explain their offering. Other regulators also have made inquiries, including ASIC.

The firm also has a substantial financial buffer to navigate any cost increases inside an emerging regulatory environment. In 2025, it reported revenues of approximately $420 million, representing a 31% year-on-year growth. “A regulated environment is a higher barrier, right? That means that there will be no hundreds of prop firms, but maybe tens of prop firms will remain,” Vašíček says.

Nonetheless, Šuffner wonders about the need to regulate simulated trading. “Regulation is here to protect the client, for good reason,” he says. “With prop firm clients, they are buying a service for a much smaller amount that they basically deposit money with a brokerage firm. So, is there even something to regulate?”

Among the most intriguing shifts currently unfolding in the space is that futures-based prop offerings are becoming a new darling for funded traders. There’s good reason: industry pricing data indicate that a $100,000 futures evaluation costs roughly $190 on average, compared with about $420 for a $100,000 CFD/FX one.

Unsurprisingly, Šuffner notes that futures “were highly requested from our clients.”

An IPO in the Horizon?

Despite record top-line growth, 2025 tested the firm's profitability. FTMO’s net income fell by 59% to roughly $37.5 million, a drop attributed to extreme market volatility. What with President Trump's dizzying tariff announcements, tech-sector anxieties and general geopolitical friction, it made predicting where the chips would fall difficult. FTMO missed its projected trader payout targets by 82%.

Interestingly, Šuffner treats this primarily as an accounting variance. “I honestly didn’t know about it. I just saw it in the articles,” he says. “It’s an accounting number, but from a company point of view is not something that would harm us in any way.”

As they navigate these market conditions, the founders are determined to conduct business on their own terms. They want to distance FTMO from the aggressive, lifestyle-focused marketing that proliferates in the industry.

“We never had aggressive marketing, never promised cars, dreams and miracles that are done in four days,” Vašíček emphasises. “For us, it is important to still stay FTMO. We are here for the long term. So we feel this sense of accountability and we want to do serious business and provide great service for the customers.”

For now, OANDA and FTMO are kept as two businesses with distinct management teams, though both founders serve as co-CEOs overseeing the overarching structure, a role Vašíček admits is demanding, yet exciting. Vašíček notes that while they are keeping an eye on new developments like prediction markets, they remain focused on their own roadmap rather than moving at the pace dictated by others. “Like every other business, we need to look around and always think about what's the future so we don't end up being dinosaurs,” he says.

Without shareholders pressing them, they have the freedom to remain patient and move to the beat of their own drum. As Šuffner highlights, “We own 100% of FTMO and OANDA.”

While the founder mentioned in 2023, during an interview with Czech media outlet SZ, that going public did not make sense at the time, they remain open to the possibility, including any other forms of outside investment.

“An FTMO ticker sounds really cool,” Šuffner says, only half-joking.

title: Coinbase Says Customer Funds Safe After Analytics Vendor Contact-Data Incident
summary: Coinbase said an incident involving analytics provider Amplitude affected contact information associated with a small subset of Coinbase customers. For.
content:
TL;DR: Coinbase said an incident involving analytics provider Amplitude affected contact information associated with a small subset of Coinbase customers. For exchange users, the practical response is to verify contact through bookmarked official channels rather than links in unexpected messages.

Coinbase said an incident involving analytics provider Amplitude affected contact information associated with a small subset of Coinbase customers. The exchange stated that its own systems had not been accessed without authorization and that customer funds remained safe. It also said affected users would receive relevant notification. Those assertions distinguish the disclosed third-party exposure from an attack that directly drained wallets or compromised exchange custody, although the company did not provide a comprehensive public breakdown of affected data fields or customer counts.

The event and the market response

Contact details can still create real security problems. Fraudsters may use an exposed email address or phone number to write convincing impersonation messages, attempt account recovery or pose as support staff. The harm often arrives after the original incident, when an attacker combines limited information with urgent payment instructions or a request to disclose authentication codes. A customer does not need to lose a private key in the initial incident to face heightened phishing risk later. Users should therefore treat unexpected security messages with care even if their account balances look normal.

Why the development matters to the crypto market

For exchange users, the practical response is to verify contact through bookmarked official channels rather than links in unexpected messages. Turning on strong authentication, reviewing recent sign-ins and being cautious about requests for recovery phrases can reduce exposure to social engineering. These are sensible precautions even when an exchange says it has not suffered a direct intrusion. The broader market takeaway is that custody security and personal-data security are related but distinct; a platform can protect assets while a vendor still leaks information.

The strongest security response usually looks operational rather than spectacular: inventory exposed systems, restrict unnecessary access, apply verified patches, monitor unusual activity and explain the incident accurately to affected users. Claims of an exploit should not be made when only a possible vulnerability has been identified. At the same time, the absence of a confirmed theft does not eliminate the need for remediation. Trust comes from a provider’s ability to document its response and maintain reliable controls across the third parties and components on which its service depends.

Regulated institutions assessing digital assets must plan for both malicious transactions and ordinary operational failure. A secure key may be unusable after a hardware problem; a correctly signed payment can still reach the wrong destination; a trusted software component may later be compromised. Defense therefore combines cryptography with governance, recovery, vendor oversight and clear human approval. A new security tool or partnership can improve one part of that system without becoming a universal solution. Asking exactly which threats are addressed is more useful than declaring the technology safe or unsafe.

What the headline does not establish

The disclosure highlights supply-chain dependence. Exchanges use outside vendors for analytics, communication, support and other services, and some of those partners may process information that is valuable to attackers. Data minimization, retention controls, vendor audits and prompt notification are therefore part of exchange security alongside cold storage and transaction signing. Coinbase’s claim that customer funds are unaffected is important, but the available information leaves limits around exact scope. It would be inappropriate to repeat unverified rumors about a precise number of impacted customers as fact.

What to watch next

Watch for a more detailed incident statement about affected fields, notification completion and remedial vendor controls. Until then, readers should avoid unverified counts and use official Coinbase support channels to assess any account-specific risk.

2026-10-30T09:45:04.697+02:00

Friday, 30/10/2026 | 07:45 GMT by Arnab Shome

  • The regulator says it is not convinced retail access to prediction markets is in the public interest.
  • Offshore prediction markets carry no Australian legal protections, and licensees that facilitate access to them keep all their licence obligations, it added.

Australia’s corporate regulator has set out its position on prediction markets, saying it is “not currently convinced” that offering them to retail clients is in the public interest.

The announcement, as issued, states ASIC’s current stance rather than a formal ban.

London's trading industry is coming home!

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said prediction market contracts have “all the features of a bet.” It described them as highly speculative, typically involving an all-or-nothing outcome tied to a particular event, a trait they share with binary options. Binary options are prohibited for retail clients in Australia.

ASIC noted that many of the underlying events have nothing to do with investment. Its examples included whether it will rain tomorrow, or whether a sporting team will win and by how many goals. The regulator said these features raise questions about whether prediction market contracts are appropriately described as investment products.

Integrity Risks and Offshore Access

ASIC also pointed to market integrity risks. These include the misuse of confidential information, market manipulation and disputes over how outcomes are determined.

The regulator addressed two groups directly. Australians who choose to access offshore prediction markets online should be aware that they do not have protections under Australian law, ASIC said. Australian financial service licensees that facilitate access to offshore prediction markets were told that all of their licence obligations under Australian law continue to apply to that activity.

Under section 798A of the Corporations Act 2001, ASIC is required to have regard to whether granting an Australian market licence would be in the public interest.

The Binary Options Precedent and the Wider Market

The position follows the regulator’s treatment of binary options. Both products involve speculating on the binary outcome of a future event. Prediction market contracts are generally offered through a market platform, while binary options are sold over the counter via brokers.

The approach also matches that of several comparable jurisdictions, including parts of Europe and the UK, where regulators have restricted access to event contracts with similar characteristics to binary options.

ASIC banned the sale of binary options to retail clients in May 2021. Finance Magnates reported that in the 13 months before the ban, 74% to 77% of active retail clients lost money trading binary options, with aggregate net losses of A$14 million. The regulator later extended the ban until 1 October 2031, restricting licensed brokers from offering the product to retail traders.

Separately, ASIC’s limits on the leverage offered to retail clients run until 23 May 2027.

Prediction markets have been expanding elsewhere in the industry. Finance Magnates reported in April that Robinhood was selectively listing contracts, avoiding markets where insider information or manipulation risks are harder to control. In the same month, US authorities charged a soldier in what was described as the first insider trading case linked to prediction markets.
